Stationary Distribution of a Markov Chain

Source: R/03_stat.R
stat.Rd

Computes stationary distribution(s) of a finite-state, time-homogeneous Markov chain.

Usage

stat(x, ...)

Arguments

x

A valid MarkovChain or StochMat object.

...

Additional arguments passed to methods. Currently unused.

Value

A StochVec (unique recurrent class), or a list of StochVec objects.

Details

For a transition matrix \(P\), a stationary distribution \(\pi\) satisfies $$\pi^\top P = \pi^\top,\qquad \sum_i \pi_i = 1,\ \pi_i \ge 0.$$ For a MarkovChain, both components are validated and the stationary distribution depends only on the transition matrix.

If the chain has a single closed communicating class, the stationary distribution is unique (though the chain may be periodic). If there are multiple closed communicating classes, stationary distributions are not unique. Every stationary distribution is a convex combination of the extremal ones, each supported on one closed class.

The Grassmann, Taksar and Heyman (1985) algorithm, also known as GTH, computes the stationary probabilities within each closed class using off-diagonal transitions.

This function returns:

  • a single StochVec if the stationary distribution is unique;

  • otherwise a list of StochVec objects, containing extremal stationary distributions of the corresponding recurrent classes.

References

Grassmann, W. K., Taksar, M. I., and Heyman, D. P. (1985). Regenerative Analysis and Steady State Distributions for Markov Chains. Operations Research, 33(5), 1107–1116. doi:10.1287/opre.33.5.1107

See also

MarkovChain(), sim(), fit()

Examples

# Choose the transition probability matrix and the initial law of the MC
a <- c(0.5, 0.5, 0)
P <- matrix(c(0.3, 0.7, 0,
              0.6, 0.1, 0.3,
              0.5, 0,   0.5), nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# Create a Markov Chain
x <- MarkovChain(a = a, P = P)

# Find Stationary distribution
pi_vec <- stat(x)

# Simulate a single trajectory of length m
m <- 1e4
traj <- sim(m, x)

# Estimate the transition probability matrix
y <- fit(traj)

# Make a list of Markov Chains
L <- MarkovChainList(list(x, y))
L[[1]]
#> Markov Chain
#>   Number of states: 3 
#> 
#>   Initial distribution (a):
#>       1   2   3 
#>     0.5 0.5 0.0 
#> 
#>   Transition matrix (P):
#>         1   2   3
#>     1 0.3 0.7 0.0
#>     2 0.6 0.1 0.3
#>     3 0.5 0.0 0.5
